nameStory: The Carmine Orbweaver gets its striking name from its deep red coloration, reminiscent of carmine dye that was historically made from crushed cochineal insects. This rich, wine-red hue makes it one of the most distinctively colored orbweavers you might encounter in New England.
description: The Carmine Orbweaver is a medium-sized orb weaver spider known for its distinctive deep red to reddish-brown coloration. Like other orbweavers, it builds the classic circular wheel-shaped webs that most people picture when they think of spider webs. This species is quite rare in New England, making any sighting a special discovery for nature enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Deep carmine red to reddish-brown coloration across the entire body, with a somewhat glossy appearance that catches light

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Classic orb web with sticky spiral threads radiating from center, typically rebuilt daily and feeling slightly tacky to gentle touch

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Rounded, bulbous abdomen typical of orbweavers, with the abdomen noticeably larger than the front body section

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in center of web during evening hours, vibrating the web when disturbed to detect threats

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized for an orbweaver, with females noticeably larger and more robust than the smaller males

habitat: Found in wooded areas and forest edges where they can anchor their webs between trees and shrubs. They prefer locations with some protection from strong winds but enough open space to build their circular webs effectively.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late spring, starting to build their characteristic orb webs as insect prey becomes more abundant.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible in their webs, actively hunting and mating during warm evenings.
seasonality.fall: Females lay egg sacs before the first frost, while adults become less active as temperatures drop and prey becomes scarce.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive harsh New England winters; the species overwinters as eggs in protected silk sacs.

funFact: Despite being found across continents from North America to Russia, the Carmine Orbweaver is so rare in New England that it's been documented only twice, making it one of our region's most elusive spiders.
confusionNotes: The deep red coloration makes this species fairly distinctive among New England orbweavers, though it could potentially be confused with other reddish orbweavers. The key difference is the uniform carmine red color rather than mixed browns and reds.
contextualKnowledge: This spider's extreme rarity in New England means that any sighting would be noteworthy for local naturalists and could represent the northern edge of its range in eastern North America.
compareHints: Since this is the only Cercidia species in our region, compare it to other orbweavers like the Common Garden Spider or Marbled Orbweaver. The Carmine Orbweaver's uniform deep red coloration sets it apart from the typical browns, yellows, and mottled patterns of most other New England orbweavers.
